# Beatwick

Every city has a sound. Beatwick is an international music-discovery platform organized by city — 30 music markets across 5 regions, each with trending tracks, artist spotlights, scene reports, venue guides, and auto-updating Spotify playlists.

- Homepage: https://beatwick.com/
- All 30 cities by region: https://beatwick.com/cities/
- All 150 artist spotlights: https://beatwick.com/artists/
- The Founder's Global 30 (the Beatwick founder's personal curation of 30 tracks, in his exact order — editorial, not official chart data; fan votes feed future movement): https://beatwick.com/charts/
- World map: https://beatwick.com/map.html
- Archive (Oct 2025–present): https://beatwick.com/archive.html
- RSS: https://beatwick.com/feed.xml
- About: https://beatwick.com/about.html
- Get Heard — submit your music: free standard queue (a human listens to every submission, in order, no timeline promised) or $10 Priority Spin (guaranteed listen + honest written feedback within 7 days, or your money back; consideration for a spotlight/social/playlist if good enough — placement never guaranteed): https://beatwick.com/submit.html

## Charts

All Beatwick charts are curated by human editors and updated weekly. They reflect what our city editors are hearing on the ground, not streaming data.

- New Orleans: The only American city where the funeral has a brass band and the parade never really ends. Jazz was born… — https://beatwick.com/cities/new-orleans.html

## Artist spotlights (150)

### North America

- Cardi B: The Bronx's Loudest Success Story (New York): From Highbridge to the top of the Hot 100 — Belcalis Almánzar turned Bronx brashness into a pop empire. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-york-cardi-b.html
- LCD Soundsystem: Brooklyn's Dance-Punk Professors (New York): James Murphy made middle-aged anxiety danceable and turned a farewell show at MSG into a resurrection. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-york-lcd-soundsystem.html
- MIKE (New York): Brooklyn's underground poet laureate — MIKE's hazy, self-produced rap runs on his own 10k label and answers to nobody. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-york-mike.html
- Nas: Queensbridge's Poet Laureate (New York): Nas turned Queensbridge into literature. Thirty years after Illmatic, New York still rhymes in his sentences. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-york-nas.html
- Water From Your Eyes (New York): Brooklyn's weirdest pop duo — Nate Amos and Rachel Brown make experimental dance music that keeps accidentally becoming everyone's favorite record. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-york-water-from-your-eyes.html
- Billie Eilish: Highland Park's Bedroom Pop Revolutionary (Los Angeles): She recorded a global takeover in her brother's bedroom. LA's strangest pop star never had to leave the neighborhood to conquer it. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/los-angeles-billie-eilish.html
- Kendrick Lamar: Compton's Conscience (Los Angeles): A Pulitzer, a Super Bowl, and the most consequential rap career of the century — all traced back to Compton. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/los-angeles-kendrick-lamar.html
- Navy Blue (Los Angeles): Los Angeles-born skater turned underground-rap confessor — Navy Blue's drumless loops and warm jazz samples carry the city's quietest fire. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/los-angeles-navy-blue.html
- Pink Siifu (Los Angeles): The most prolific shape-shifter in underground rap — Pink Siifu's GUMBO'! folds jazz, punk, and Southern rap into one simmering pot. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/los-angeles-pink-siifu.html
- Snoop Dogg: Long Beach's Coolest Export (Los Angeles): Discovered by Dr. Dre, immortal by thirty, and still the smoothest voice in rap. Uncle Snoop is LA's permanent ambassador. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/los-angeles-snoop-dogg.html
- Alessia Cara: Brampton's Quiet Storm (Toronto): She sang about hating parties and won a Grammy. The GTA's most honest voice never had to shout. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/toronto-alessia-cara.html
- Drake: The 6 God Built Toronto's Music Economy (Toronto): Before Drake, Toronto was a feeder market. Then the kid from Degrassi turned the 6ix into a global sound. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/toronto-drake.html
- LOONY (Toronto): Scarborough's neo-soul secret — LOONY's JOYRiDE and soft thing earned Polaris longlists, Elton John's obsession, and a Metro Boomin sample. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/toronto-loony.html
- River Tiber (Toronto): Toronto's ghostwriter-in-plain-sight — River Tiber's falsetto has been sampled by Drake and Kendrick while his own records stay beautifully under the radar. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/toronto-river-tiber.html
- The Weeknd: Toronto After Dark (Toronto): From anonymous Scarborough mixtapes to the biggest song of the streaming era — Abel Tesfaye made the night sound expensive. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/toronto-the-weeknd.html
- Arcade Fire: Montreal's Indie-Rock Miracle (Montréal): A funeral that became a coronation: how a Montreal collective took Funeral from Mile End lofts to a Grammy for Album of the Year. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/montreal-arcade-fire.html
- Céline Dion: Quebec's Voice of the Century (Montréal): From Charlemagne to the world stage — the francophone powerhouse who became the best-selling artist Canada ever produced. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/montreal-celine-dion.html
- KAYTRANADA: Montreal's Groove Scientist (Montréal): From Haitian roots to Montreal basements to a Grammy — the producer who taught the world to dance at 100 BPM. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/montreal-kaytranada.html
- Lydia Képinski (Montréal): Montreal's francophone chaos-pop queen — Lydia Képinski turned a Francouvertes win into two Polaris-longlisted albums of pure theatrical pop. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/montreal-lydia-kepinski.html
- Ouri (Montréal): A classically trained cellist in Montreal's rave scene — Ouri fuses orchestral composition and electronic grit into something nobody else makes. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/montreal-ouri.html
- Becca Mancari (Nashville): East Nashville's genre escape artist — Becca Mancari went from Americana darling to polyrhythmic pop on the self-produced Left Hand. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/nashville-becca-mancari.html
- Chris Stapleton: Nashville's Songwriter Who Stepped Forward (Nashville): He wrote the hits for everyone else. Then Traveller made him the most respected voice in country music. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/nashville-chris-stapleton.html
- Dolly Parton: Nashville's Patron Saint (Nashville): She arrived in Nashville the day after high school graduation with a guitar and a plan. The city never stood a chance. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/nashville-dolly-parton.html
- Jack White: Nashville's Rock-and-Roll Contrarian (Nashville): The Detroit garage-rocker who moved his whole operation to Nashville and built the city's loudest independent institution. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/nashville-jack-white.html
- Madi Diaz (Nashville): Nashville's indie-folk survivor — Madi Diaz took 14 years, an ANTI- deal, and Harry Styles' tour band to get her due. History of a Feeling explains it all. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/nashville-madi-diaz.html
- Anycia (Atlanta): Atlanta's independent princess of trap — Anycia went viral on 'So What', self-released Princess Pop That, and never signed a deal. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/atlanta-anycia.html
- Outkast: Atlanta Invented the Future Twice (Atlanta): André 3000 and Big Boi turned East Point into the center of the hip-hop universe — and told the South it had something to say. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/atlanta-outkast.html
- Slimesito (Atlanta): Clayton County's bilingual plugg ghost — Slimesito has run Atlanta's underground since the SoundCloud era, no label deal in sight. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/atlanta-slimesito.html
- T.I.: The King of the South Holds Court (Atlanta): He named the genre, then ruled it. Bankhead's finest made trap a global language. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/atlanta-ti.html
- Usher: Atlanta's King of R&B (Atlanta): He moved to Atlanta as a teenager and never left the throne. Thirty years later, the Confessions still haven't been topped. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/atlanta-usher.html
- Big Freedia: The Queen of Bounce (New Orleans): She took New Orleans bounce from the housing projects to Beyoncé's Formation. The Queen diva remains undefeated. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-orleans-big-freedia.html
- HaSizzle (New Orleans): The self-proclaimed King of Bounce — HaSizzle's voice is New Orleans' secret weapon, sampled by Drake and storming Coachella. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-orleans-hasizzle.html
- Lil Wayne: New Orleans' Prodigy Who Never Left (New Orleans): Signed to Cash Money at nine, running rap by twenty-five. Hollygrove's greatest export turned work ethic into mythology. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-orleans-lil-wayne.html
- Mia Borders (New Orleans): New Orleans' independent soul queen — Mia Borders has released nine records on her own Blaxican Records, from Tipitina's to the Louisiana Philharmonic. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-orleans-mia-borders.html
- Trombone Shorty: Treme's Brass-Band Ambassador (New Orleans): Troy Andrews was leading brass bands at six. Now he's the man who carries New Orleans' second-line tradition to the world. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/new-orleans-trombone-shorty.html

### Latin America & Caribbean

- Criolo (São Paulo): São Paulo's conscience with a microphone — rap that sounds like rain on concrete. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/sao-paulo-criolo.html
- Emicida (São Paulo): The battle-rap killer who built an empire and named an album after hope. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/sao-paulo-emicida.html
- MC Luanna (São Paulo): From São Paulo's baile circuit to shared bills with rap legends — MC Luanna makes lean, lethal funk that blew up track by track on her own terms. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/sao-paulo-mc-luanna.html
- Rita Lee (São Paulo): The queen of Brazilian rock — São Paulo's own, from Tropicália to eternity. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/sao-paulo-rita-lee.html
- Tasha & Tracie (São Paulo): São Paulo's twin rap queens stitch funk carioca to trap and rap, rhyming about Black culture, the periphery, and pure self-esteem — with Ludmilla, Djonga, and Gloria… — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/sao-paulo-tasha-tracie.html
- Café Tacvba (Mexico City): Four kids from Satélite who became the most inventive band in rock en español. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/mexico-city-cafe-tacvba.html
- Foudeqush (Mexico City): Mexico City's alt-soul voice went from the capital's scene to the Black Panther: Wakanda Forever soundtrack — and her own album ANGELA is where the story really starts. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/mexico-city-foudeqush.html
- Meth Math (Mexico City): Three friends from Hermosillo who met making a horror film now run Mexico City's most cursed perreo — satanic, deconstructed reggaetón from the capital's DIY underground. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/mexico-city-meth-math.html
- Natalia Lafourcade (Mexico City): Mexico City's folk-song surgeon — intimate, precise, and quietly unstoppable. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/mexico-city-natalia-lafourcade.html
- Zoé (Mexico City): Mexico City's psychedelic romantics who proved the Unplugged format had a pulse. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/mexico-city-zoe.html
- Aterciopelados (Bogotá): Bogotá's alt-rock weirdos who made Andean weirdness anthemic. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/bogota-aterciopelados.html
- Bomba Estéreo (Bogotá): The Bogotá collective that turned Caribbean futurism into a global export. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/bogota-bomba-estereo.html
- Ghetto Kumbé (Bogotá): A masked trio from Colombia's coast turned Bogotá into their ritual ground — Afro-Caribbean drums folded into house, hip-hop, and bass on ZZK Records, with masks on and… — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/bogota-ghetto-kumbe.html
- Las Añez (Bogotá): Twin sisters from Bogotá, two loop stations, and Colombian folk bent into impossible shapes — Las Añez have award-winning albums, Andrea Echeverri features, and… — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/bogota-las-anez.html
- Monsieur Periné (Bogotá): Bogotá's swing-era dreamers who smuggled cumbia into a Parisian jazz club. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/bogota-monsieur-perine.html
- Bizarrap (Buenos Aires): The producer in the cap who turned a bedroom studio into Argentina's biggest export machine. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/buenos-aires-bizarrap.html
- Duki (Buenos Aires): From the Parque Rivadavia rap battles to the top of Latin trap — Almagro's favorite son. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/buenos-aires-duki.html
- Fin del Mundo (Buenos Aires): Buenos Aires' all-female shoegaze revelation — dreamy post-rock apocalypses, KEXP and Radio 3 spins, a first European tour, and an album called Todo Va Hacia el Mar. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/buenos-aires-fin-del-mundo.html
- Six Sex (Buenos Aires): The Buenos Aires club queen who invented ravetón — reggaetón dragged through the rave — went from SoundCloud experiments to Remezcla's #1 dance song of 2024 and a debut… — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/buenos-aires-six-sex.html
- Soda Stereo (Buenos Aires): The trio that made Buenos Aires the capital of Spanish-language rock. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/buenos-aires-soda-stereo.html
- Bob Marley (Kingston): The prophet of Trench Town who made a tiny island's music the planet's second language. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/kingston-bob-marley.html
- Iotosh (Kingston): The three-time Grammy-nominated producer behind Koffee's West Indies and Jah9's Note to Self stepped out from behind the boards — Kingston's Iotosh is an artist now. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/kingston-iotosh.html
- Mortimer (Kingston): Kingston's most honest new reggae voice took a decade to make his debut — then dropped From Within, with Damian Marley, Kabaka Pyramid, and Lila Iké on the tracklist. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/kingston-mortimer.html
- Sean Paul (Kingston): Kingston's dancehall ambassador who made the whole world say 'dutty yeah'. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/kingston-sean-paul.html
- Vybz Kartel (Kingston): The Worl' Boss — dancehall's most prolific mind, back where he belongs: on stage. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/kingston-vybz-kartel.html

### Europe

- Adele (London): Tottenham's once-in-a-generation voice — the BRIT School graduate who outsold everyone and stayed herself. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/london-adele.html
- Jim Legxacy (London): Catford's one-man genre blender wrote the decade's biggest UK rap hit, then signed to XL and made the weirdest, best record of 2025 anyway. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/london-jim-legxacy.html
- Odeal (London): The London alté crooner who turned a bedroom recording into a global R&B redefinition — LVRN signed, MOBO blessed, and still making it up in the studio. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/london-odeal.html
- Skepta (London): The Tottenham MC who carried grime on his back for a decade — then made it the world's problem. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/london-skepta.html
- Stormzy (London): The South London MC who took grime from YouTube freestyles to Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/london-stormzy.html
- Ellen Allien (Berlin): BPitch Control's founder wrote the love letter Berlin's techno scene deserved — then spent 25 years running its best label. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/berlin-ellen-allien.html
- Moderat (Berlin): Two Berlin electronic institutions plus one ghostly voice — the supergroup that made techno cry. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/berlin-moderat.html
- Nene H (Berlin): Berlin-via-Istanbul funky techno with a heart — the UMAY founder whose grief record Ali became one of the underground's most honest albums. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/berlin-nene-h.html
- Paul Kalkbrenner (Berlin): Berlin's techno everyman — the DJ who carried the city's sound from the Bunker to the big screen. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/berlin-paul-kalkbrenner.html
- Ziúr (Berlin): The Berlin producer turning grindcore drums and smashing glass into club weapons — Planet Mu's most confrontational export, and the co-founder of the Boo Hoo night. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/berlin-ziur.html
- Aya Nakamura (Paris): The banlieue singer who made French the language of global R&B — one 'Djadja' at a time. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/paris-aya-nakamura.html
- Benjamin Epps (Paris): The Gabonese-born Paris MC keeping boom bap alive with a Jadakiss intro, a BET Hip Hop Award, and the sharpest French-language pen of his generation. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/paris-benjamin-epps.html
- Booba (Paris): French rap's undisputed heavyweight — three decades deep and still the name every new MC has to answer to. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/paris-booba.html
- Daft Punk (Paris): Two Parisians in robot helmets taught the whole planet to dance in French — then vanished at the height of their powers. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/paris-daft-punk.html
- Yoa (Paris): Paris' electro-pop prodigy went from theater kid to Victoires de la Musique revelation — La Favorite is the most fun French pop record in years. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/paris-yoa.html
- Afrojack (Amsterdam): Spijkenisse's wall of sound — the producer who made Dutch house hit like a truck and never turned it down. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/amsterdam-afrojack.html
- Tiësto (Amsterdam): The Breda kid who took trance to the Olympics and became the first DJ to outgrow the club entirely. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/amsterdam-dj-tiesto.html
- Martin Garrix (Amsterdam): The kid from Amstelveen who released 'Animals' at 17 and never left the top of dance music again. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/amsterdam-martin-garrix.html
- Tracey (Amsterdam): Tom Ruijg makes house and electro like a love letter to Detroit — the Amsterdam producer whose Skyfall rewired the Voyage Direct faithful. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/amsterdam-tracey.html
- upsammy (Amsterdam): Amsterdam's IDM naturalist turns melting ice and rustling leaves into Dekmantel-certified electronica — the De School residency that became a career. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/amsterdam-upsammy.html
- Bad Gyal (Barcelona): The Vilassar de Mar singer who took dancehall to Catalonia — and made Barcelona the capital of Spanish perreo. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/barcelona-bad-gyal.html
- Julieta (Barcelona): The Barcelona engineer-turned-pop auteur who self-produced her way from GarageBand to Primavera Sound — Catalan club romanticism at its finest. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/barcelona-julieta.html
- Mushkaa (Barcelona): Bad Gyal's little sister became Catalan urbano's most self-reliant star — self-released, singing in Catalan, and headlining festivals on her own terms. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/barcelona-mushkaa.html
- Rigoberta Bandini (Barcelona): Barcelona's theater kid turned pop provocateur — the voice that made 'Ay Mamá' a national anthem. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/barcelona-rigoberta-bandini.html
- Rosalía (Barcelona): A Catalan flamenco student rewired pop in three languages — and made Barcelona the center of the Latin avant-garde. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/barcelona-rosalia.html
- Buraka Som Sistema (Lisbon): The Lisbon collective that turned Angolan kuduro into a global club weapon — and made the suburbs the city's sound. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lisbon-buraka-som-sistema.html
- Mariza (Lisbon): Fado's global ambassador — raised in Mouraria, the Lisbon quarter where the music was born. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lisbon-mariza.html
- Nídia Minaj (Lisbon): The kuduro queen of Príncipe Discos who learned beat-making from YouTube tutorials and became Lisbon's most explosive electronic export. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lisbon-nidia-minaj.html
- Papillon (Lisbon): The Sintra-line MC who turned underdog status into a sold-out Coliseu — Lisbon's most thoughtful rapper, three albums deep on his own label. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lisbon-papillon.html
- Salvador Sobral (Lisbon): The jazz singer who won Eurovision by whispering — and gave Portugal its first victory. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lisbon-salvador-sobral.html
- ABBA (Stockholm): Stockholm's most successful export isn't furniture — it's four Swedes in platform boots who wrote the pop playbook. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/stockholm-abba.html
- Avicii (Stockholm): The Stockholm producer who made EDM cry, sing, and feel something — gone at 28, still everywhere. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/stockholm-avicii.html
- GRANT (Stockholm): The Swedish indie-pop dramatist from a farm outside Stockholm whose Waterline earned a Grammis nod and a P3 Gold Future Artist crown. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/stockholm-grant.html
- Maja Francis (Stockholm): Sweden's 'Emo Dolly Parton' — the Stockholm indie-pop songwriter whose Anxious Angel closed Netflix's Love & Anarchy and whose Mama enlisted First Aid Kit. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/stockholm-maja-francis.html
- Robyn (Stockholm): Pop's patron saint of crying in the club — Stockholm's Robyn wrote the blueprint and never needed the crown. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/stockholm-robyn.html
- Belle and Sebastian (Glasgow): The shyest band in Glasgow became its most beloved — twee as a weapon, melodies as armor. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/glasgow-belle-sebastian.html
- Franz Ferdinand (Glasgow): Four art-school misfits who turned Glasgow's post-punk attic into the biggest guitar band of the 2000s. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/glasgow-franz-ferdinand.html
- Humour (Glasgow): Glasgow's feistiest post-punk quintet — NME-approved chaos, surreal lyrics, and a debut album Learning Greek that made the weirdness official. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/glasgow-humour.html
- Mogwai (Glasgow): Glasgow's loudest quiet band — five post-rock architects who built their own label and never looked back. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/glasgow-mogwai.html
- VLURE (Glasgow): Glasgow's trance-punk five-piece went from sticky indie venues to a Bobby Gillespie collaboration — Escalate is the sound of the city's subterranean dancefloors. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/glasgow-vlure.html

### Africa & Middle East

- Asake (Lagos): Mr. Money fused Lagos street fuji with amapiano's log drum and became the fastest-rising star of the decade. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lagos-asake.html
- Ayo Maff (Lagos): From the Bariga streets of Lagos to a chart-topping link-up with Fireboy DML — the self-styled Prince of the Street carrying street-hop into a new generation. — https://beatwick.com/spotlights/lagos-ayo-maff.html
